claims.text: As-deposited nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy films or nanoribbons have high residual stress, defect concentrations, and grain-boundary irregularities.
Spatially heterogeneous residual stresses and defect distributions create local variations in the energy barriers for a magnetostructural phase transition.
Microstructural inhomogeneities govern the magnitude of the magnetocaloric effect in these nanoscale alloys.
Microstructural inhomogeneities govern hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
A short anneal at approximately 300 °C can relieve internal stresses without causing excessive grain growth.
Stress-relief annealing reduces defect and strain inhomogeneity.
Grain boundaries, defect density, and localized strain fields mediate nucleation of the magnetostructural phase transition.
High defect and strain concentrations cause spatially non-uniform nucleation of the magnetostructural transition.
Spatially non-uniform nucleation broadens the transition-temperature range.
Spatially non-uniform nucleation enhances hysteresis through latent-heat trapping.
Annealing enables a more uniform and rapid magnetostructural transition during magnetic cycling.
Annealed samples will exhibit a sharper magnetic transition than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit a reduced hysteresis width relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will produce a magnetocaloric peak that more closely approaches the anticipated thermodynamic value.
Reducing defect-mediated nucleation barriers improves heat dissipation during rapid cycling.
Latent-heat release imposes consequential heat-transfer limitations in low-field cycling of nanoscale films or nanoribbons.
The proposed behavior applies at magnetic fields below 100 mT.
The annealing treatment must avoid materially changing phase composition or crystallite size beyond stress relaxation.
